intro: How the writing becomes a job rather than a hobby. Cadence, promotion and positioning — plus the build ideas that are content in their own right.

groups.title: The publishing loop
groups.note: One piece of work, four artifacts. The premise that makes this sustainable: everything published comes out of something you actually did, so the research is already paid for.

items.d: A measurement, a finding or a bug is the input. A topic picked without one produces an article with nothing true in it.

items.t: Three depths on one piece of work
items.d: Beginner: the idea that made it make sense. Intermediate: the walkthrough with code that runs. Advanced: what surprised you, which only you can write.

items.t: The canonical article, then the adaptations
items.d: Long form on the site is the canonical version; the thread, the newsletter and the video all point back to it.

items.t: Weekly cadence that survives a bad week
items.d: One advanced piece a fortnight, one intermediate in between, beginner pieces only when they fall out of the other two.

items.t: Run every draft through the writing check
items.d: POST /api/writing/check before publishing. Block-level findings fail; the judgement calls come back as questions.

groups.title: Promotion: the thread and the newsletter
groups.note: Generated as structure by content/topics.py --promote. The structure is automated; the words are not, because a generated thread reads exactly like one.

items.t: Open with the finding, not with 'a thread'
items.d: The first post is the number or the surprise. If it is not interesting without the rest, the rest will not be read.
Each post should be the claim you could not have made before doing the work.
What you expected versus what happened. This is the post that gets quoted.

items.t: Show the method briefly so it is checkable
items.d: Credibility comes from being falsifiable, not from confidence.

items.t: Last post links the article, and nothing else
items.d: No 'follow for more'. The link is the call to action.

items.t: Newsletter subject: the finding in under nine words
items.d: No colon-subtitle construction. The intro is the one sentence that makes someone open the article.
A thread that opens with something your audience already knows spends the attention it just earned.

groups.title: Positioning: twenty-four weeks to top-1% candidate
groups.note: The plan behind the writing. Weeks 1-8 depth, 9-16 portfolio, 17-24 visibility.

items.d: Upgradeable patterns, fail-safes — circuit breakers and pausability — and a library of reusable secure modules you actually reuse.
Deploy the same contract to Ethereum, Arbitrum, Optimism, Polygon and Solana. Build a demo bridge. Document the latency, fee and security trade-offs.
Run your own node. Automate deployment with CI. Stand up monitoring in Grafana, Tenderly and Dune.

items.t: Weeks 9-16, project 1: a DeFi protocol with fail-safe architecture
items.d: Lending and borrowing with a circuit breaker and oracle integration. Document how liquidity drains are prevented — this is where the audit background shows.
An Ethereum to Solana transfer over Wormhole or LayerZero, with the risk analysis written alongside.

items.t: Weeks 9-16, project 3: an enterprise use case
items.d: Supply chain or identity on IPFS plus contracts, integrated with a Web2 API, to prove you can bridge both worlds.
A public repo with a clean README and architecture diagram, a technical post explaining the design decisions, and a demo video.
Deep dives on your own projects, architecture commentary where your peers are, and a talk at a meetup or hackathon.

items.t: Weeks 17-24: networking that is not asking for things
items.d: Be where solutions engineers already are. Offer free architecture reviews to small projects — credibility compounds faster than applications.
Protocol teams, L2s and infra providers. Lead the CV with system design and integration rather than with languages.

items.t: Security plus architecture is the combination
items.d: Very few engineers pair audit-level security with solution design. Market that pairing explicitly rather than listing both separately.
Compliance basics — KYC/AML, GDPR, token regulation — are what make you valuable to companies crossing from Web2.
'Web3 architecture playbooks' and 'secure design patterns for DeFi' as named, reusable assets rather than one-off posts.
Projects and experiments. This is what produces the evidence everything else depends on.
Whitepapers and protocol docs, not feeds.
Documenting what you learned, publicly. The compounding habit.
A comment, a message or a shared insight. One is enough if it is every day.

items.t: A chatbot with the Vercel AI SDK, LangGraph, Supabase and Next.js
items.d: A full-stack AI build that doubles as the deployment half of the AI roadmap.

items.t: Webhooks versus APIs, explained with your own migration
items.d: You replaced polling with webhooks and have the bill. Use the real numbers.

items.t: An AI bug bounty agent, in public
items.d: Build it, measure it, and publish the misses. The single most credible thing you can ship this year.
Small, useful, and the kind of tool that gets starred and cited.

items.t: A gas cost translator: gas to ETH to USD to cost-per-user
items.d: The calculator every product team wants and nobody has built well.
